english: haha / lol — laughter sound, from 크크 / 큭큭 (the giggle/snicker sound). The most-used reaction in Korean chats. (casual slang — fine with friends, never in formal work messages)
usage: stands for 크크, just casual laughing
a lone ㅋ (often typed ㅋ..) can read as dry or unimpressed — careful
examples: 나 오늘 지하철 놓쳐서 회사 지각함 ㅋㅋㅋ
I missed the subway and was late to work today lol
laughing at your own bad luck to a friend
방금 보낸 짤 개웃겨 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ
The meme you just sent is so funny hahaha
reacting to a meme in a group chat
A: 나 또 소개팅 망함 / B: ㅋㅋㅋ 왜ㅠㅠ
A: My blind date flopped again / B: hahaha whyy
teasing a friend gently
nuance: ㅋㅋ is the default friendly laugh among Korean 20-30s and reads as warm and relaxed; more ㅋ means louder laughing. Use it freely with friends, dates, and close coworkers, but keep it out of formal messages to a boss, professor, or a stranger you just met. Be careful with a lone ㅋ — to some people it can feel cold or sarcastic, so when in doubt use at least ㅋㅋ.
mistakes: Sending a single ㅋ to someone sensitive — it can read as cold or annoyed, so use ㅋㅋ or more

english: hehe / soft smile — gentle laughter, from 흐흐 / 하하 (a soft chuckle). Softer and warmer than ㅋㅋ. (casual slang — friendly, but mild enough that it edges into okay with friendly coworkers)
usage: stands for 흐흐, a soft warm laugh
softens a reply so it is not blunt
warm, used even with friendly coworkers
examples: 오늘 도와주셔서 감사했어요 ㅎㅎ
Thanks for your help today hehe
softening a thank-you to a friendly senior coworker
주말에 시간 되면 같이 카페 갈래? ㅎㅎ
If you are free this weekend wanna go to a cafe together? hehe
asking gently so it is not pushy
A: 나 요리 처음 해봤어 / B: 오 잘했네 ㅎㅎ
A: I cooked for the first time / B: oh nice job hehe
warm encouragement to a friend
nuance: ㅎㅎ is the soft, smiley cousin of ㅋㅋ; it sounds gentle and polite rather than full belly-laugh funny. Koreans often add it to soften a short reply so it does not feel cold, which is why it sneaks into messages with friendly coworkers more than ㅋㅋ does. Still, in a strictly formal message to a boss or stranger, drop it.
mistakes: Thinking ㅎㅎ means something is very funny — it is a soft smile, not a big laugh like ㅋㅋㅋ

english: yeah / yep — casual yes, from 응응 (the casual 응 = yeah). A quick agreement. (casual slang — only with friends or close peers, never to a boss or elder)
examples: A: 이따 7시에 강남역에서 봐 / B: ㅇㅇ 거기서 봐
A: See you at Gangnam Station at 7 / B: yep see you there
confirming a meetup with a friend
A: 너 그 드라마 봤어? / B: ㅇㅇ 어제 다 봤어
A: Did you watch that drama? / B: yeah I finished it yesterday
casual reply in a chat
A: 배달 치킨 시킬까? / B: ㅇㅇㅇㅇ 콜
A: Should we order delivery chicken? / B: yesss deal
excited agreement among friends
nuance: ㅇㅇ is the texted version of the casual 응 (yeah), so it carries the same banmal (informal) feeling and is only for friends, dating partners, or peers your age. Sending ㅇㅇ to a boss, professor, or older stranger is rude because it skips all politeness — use 네 or 네네 there instead. Among close friends it is fast, friendly, and totally normal.
mistakes: Replying ㅇㅇ to a boss or older person instead of 네 — it sounds blunt and disrespectful

english: nope / nah — casual no, from 노노 (English no-no) or 'nono'. A quick, light refusal. (casual slang — friends only, never to a boss or elder)
usage: stands for 노노, light casual no
examples: A: 너 이번 주말에 약속 있어? / B: ㄴㄴ 완전 한가해
A: Do you have plans this weekend? / B: nope totally free
letting a friend know you are available
A: 이 카페 너가 가보자고 한 데 맞지? / B: ㄴㄴ 그 옆 건물이야
A: This is the cafe you suggested right? / B: no it's the building next to it
correcting gently
A: 오늘 술 한잔 할래? / B: ㄴㄴ 나 내일 출근이라 패스ㅠ
A: Wanna grab a drink today? / B: nah I work tomorrow so I'll pass
declining drinks to a friend
nuance: ㄴㄴ is a light, friendly no — much softer and more playful than a flat refusal, which is exactly why it stays among friends and peers. Because it is built from casual speech, never fire it at a boss or older stranger; soften to 아니요 or 아닙니다 there. With friends it is the natural quick way to say nope without sounding harsh.
mistakes: Using ㄴㄴ in a work chat — it is too casual; write 아니요 or 아닙니다 to seniors

english: let's go / go for it — from 고고 (English go-go). Used to say 'let's do it / let's head out / start now.' (casual slang — friends and peers; too breezy for a boss)
usage: stands for 고고, let us start or head out
examples: A: 새로 생긴 술집 갈까? / B: ㄱㄱㄱ 지금 출발
A: Wanna hit the new bar? / B: let's gooo leaving now
hyping up plans with friends
A: 게임 한 판 더? / B: ㄱㄱ
A: One more game? / B: let's go
agreeing to keep playing
A: 점심 국밥 어때 / B: ㅇㅇ 바로 ㄱㄱ
A: How about gukbap for lunch / B: yeah let's go right now
deciding lunch with a coworker friend
nuance: ㄱㄱ is an energetic 'let's go / let's start,' borrowed from gaming and now used for any plan — heading out, ordering food, starting a task. It feels hype and breezy, so keep it for friends and casual peers; with a boss say something like 바로 진행하겠습니다 instead. It often pairs with ㅇㅋ or ㅇㅇ to lock in a plan.
mistakes: Reading ㄱㄱ as just 'good' — it means 고고 (let's go), not 'good good'

english: sorry / my bad — short for 죄송 (from 죄송해요, sorry). A quick light apology. (casual slang — friends and peers only; NEVER as a real apology to a boss or elder)
examples: A: 너 어제 내 카톡 안 읽었지 / B: 헐 ㅈㅅㅈㅅ 진짜 못 봤어
A: You ignored my KakaoTalk yesterday right / B: omg sorry sorry I really didn't see it
apologizing to a friend
나 5분 정도 늦을 듯 ㅈㅅ ㅠㅠ
I'll be like 5 minutes late my bad
warning a friend you are running late
A: 그거 내 거였는데 / B: 아 ㅈㅅ 몰랐어
A: That was mine / B: oh my bad I didn't know
quick casual apology to a peer
nuance: ㅈㅅ is a light, casual 'my bad' for tiny slip-ups among friends — being a little late, missing a text, taking the wrong cup. Because it shrinks a serious word (죄송) into two letters, it sounds too flippant for a real apology; never send ㅈㅅ to a boss, professor, or older stranger. For them, write the full 죄송합니다 or 죄송해요.
mistakes: Sending ㅈㅅ to a boss or for a serious mistake — it sounds careless; use 죄송합니다 fully

english: congrats — short for 축하 (from 축하해, congratulations). A quick congratulation. (casual slang — friends and peers; for elders or bosses write it out fully)
usage: mixing the abbreviation into a sentence
examples: A: 나 드디어 취업했어!! / B: 헐 ㅊㅋㅊㅋㅊㅋ 한턱 쏴
A: I finally got a job!! / B: omg congrats congrats treat me
celebrating a friend landing a job
A: 우리 이번 달에 이사 가 / B: 오 ㅊㅋ 집들이 언제?
A: We're moving this month / B: oh congrats when's the housewarming?
reacting to a friend's news
생일 ㅊㅋ!! 선물은 만나서 줄게 ㅎㅎ
Happy bday!! I'll give your gift when we meet hehe
casual birthday wishes to a friend
nuance: ㅊㅋ is the quick texted form of 축하 (congrats) and feels cheerful and informal, perfect for friends celebrating jobs, birthdays, moves, or relationships. Because it abbreviates a warm word into letters, it can feel too offhand for someone you respect; to a boss, professor, or older relative write 축하드려요 or 축하합니다 in full. Among friends it is the normal fast way to cheer someone on.
mistakes: Texting ㅊㅋ to a senior for something important — write out 축하드려요 to show real sincerity

romanization: yuyu (the letters yu-yu; read as a crying-face emoticon, not spoken)
english: crying emoticon — ㅠㅠ or ㅜㅜ looks like teary eyes. Shows sadness, frustration, or playful whining. (casual slang — friends and peers; not for formal messages)
usage: the ㅠ shape looks like falling tears
single one for a small sad sigh
examples: 오늘 야근 또 해ㅠㅠ 집 가고 싶어
I have to work overtime again todayy I wanna go home
venting to a friend after work
A: 그 카페 오늘 휴무래 / B: 헐 진짜?ㅠㅠ 가고 싶었는데
A: That cafe is closed today / B: omg really? I wanted to go
disappointed reaction to a friend
나 지갑 잃어버림ㅠㅠㅠㅠ 카드 다 정지해야 돼
I lost my walletttt I have to cancel all my cards
upset venting in a group chat
nuance: ㅠㅠ (and the twin ㅜㅜ) draws crying eyes and is one of the most common emotional markers in Korean chat; more of them means more dramatic, often half-joking sadness or whining. It is warm and expressive among friends and dating partners, but leave it out of formal or work messages where it looks unprofessional. Koreans use it for everything from genuine sadness to playful 'aw man.'
mistakes: Putting ㅠㅠ in a formal email or message to a boss — it reads as childish there

english: for real / fr — short for 리얼 (English 'real'). Means 'seriously / no joke / I agree it's true.' (casual slang — friends and peers, common among young people)
usage: agreeing while laughing, very common combo
dropping it into a sentence as 'really'
examples: A: 요즘 월세 너무 비싸 / B: ㄹㅇ 미쳤어 진짜
A: Rent is so expensive these days / B: for real it's insane
strongly agreeing with a friend about rent
A: 그 신상 카페 사람 진짜 많더라 / B: ㄹㅇㅋㅋ 웨이팅 한 시간
A: That new cafe was so packed / B: fr lol the wait was an hour
agreeing about a crowded cafe
A: 나 어제 연예인 봤어 / B: ㄹㅇ? 누구?!
A: I saw a celebrity yesterday / B: for real? who?!
reacting with surprise
nuance: ㄹㅇ (from 리얼/real) is a go-to way for young Koreans to say 'for real / no joke,' either agreeing hard with someone or asking 'seriously?' It is very current slang among 20-30s and feels natural in friend chats and comments, often paired as ㄹㅇㅋㅋ. Keep it casual-only; in work or formal contexts use 진짜요 or 정말요 instead.
mistakes: Confusing ㄹㅇ with 'right now' — it means 'for real / really,' from 리얼

english: bye bye — from 바이바이 (English 'bye-bye'). A quick casual goodbye to end a chat. (casual slang — friends and peers; not for closing a formal message)
examples: 나 이제 자야 됨 내일 일찍 출근ㅠㅠ ㅂㅂ
I gotta sleep now early work tomorrow bye
ending a night chat with a friend
A: 나 버스 왔다 가야 돼 / B: ㅇㅋ ㅂㅂ 조심히 가
A: My bus is here gotta go / B: ok bye get home safe
saying bye as a friend leaves
오늘 진짜 재밌었어 ㅎㅎ 다음에 또 보자 ㅂㅂ
Today was so fun hehe let's hang again bye
wrapping up after meeting friends
nuance: ㅂㅂ (from 바이바이) is a breezy, friendly 'bye' for closing a casual chat with friends, peers, or a dating partner. It is light and a little cute, so it fits informal goodbyes but not a polite sign-off to a boss or stranger — there you would write 들어가세요 or 안녕히 계세요. It often appears with ㅇㅋ or 잘 자 to wrap things up warmly.
mistakes: Ending a work message with ㅂㅂ — use a proper closing like 들어가세요 or 수고하셨습니다 instead

english: agreed / true that — short for 인정 (acknowledge/admit). Means 'I agree, that's facts.' (casual slang — friends and peers, very popular with young people)
usage: stacking two slang words for emphasis
examples: A: 평일에 데이트하는 게 사람도 없고 더 좋아 / B: ㅇㅈㅇㅈ 주말은 너무 붐벼
A: Weekday dates are better, less crowded / B: totally agree weekends are too packed
agreeing with a dating opinion
A: 회사 근처 그 국밥집이 제일 가성비 좋음 / B: ㅇㅈ ㄹㅇ 자주 감
A: That gukbap place near work has the best value / B: agreed for real I go often
agreeing with a coworker friend
A: 이 노래 올해 띵곡이야 / B: ㅇㅈ 진짜 명곡
A: This song is the bop of the year / B: agreed it's a real classic
agreeing about music
nuance: ㅇㅈ comes from 인정 ('I acknowledge / admit it') and is a super-common way for young Koreans to say 'agreed, that's facts.' It feels punchy and current, great for friend chats and comments, and often stacks with ㄹㅇ for emphasis. Keep it casual; in a formal setting say 맞아요 or 동의해요 instead.
mistakes: Using ㅇㅈ in formal writing — it is slang; write 동의합니다 or 맞습니다 to seniors

english: it's fine / no worries — short for 괜찮아 (it's okay). Reassures or declines softly. (casual slang — friends and peers; for formal use, write it out fully)
examples: A: 나 때문에 약속 늦어서 미안ㅠㅠ / B: ㄱㅊㄱㅊ 나도 방금 도착함
A: Sorry I made us late because of meㅠ / B: it's totally fine I just got here too
reassuring a friend
A: 내 거 음료 좀 마실래? / B: ㄱㅊ 나 방금 마셨어
A: Wanna sip my drink? / B: I'm good I just drank
softly declining
A: 어제 술 많이 마셨잖아 ㄱㅊ? / B: ㅇㅇ 멀쩡해 ㅋㅋ
A: You drank a lot yesterday, you good? / B: yeah I'm totally fine lol
checking on a friend after drinking
nuance: ㄱㅊ shrinks 괜찮아 ('it's okay') into two letters and works the same three ways — reassuring someone, saying you are fine, or softly turning something down. It is friendly and casual, ideal for friends and peers; with a boss or older person write the full 괜찮아요 or 괜찮습니다. It pairs naturally with apologies like ㅈㅅ to wave them off warmly.
mistakes: Replying ㄱㅊ to a senior's concern — say 괜찮아요 or 괜찮습니다 fully to stay polite
